title: Promises, Not Proofs
subtitle: How a program becomes a hand-wired neural network, told in the things people were sure of
logline: Handwired lets you write a JavaScript interface as builder code that becomes a neural network with every weight written by hand. It runs every operation every frame, cannot stop early, and matches JavaScript exactly, as long as nobody lies to it. Told through the beliefs tied onto its wires like paper tags (who tied each one on, who doubted it, how long it held), the film teaches how the machine really computes: two ramps for every if, a clockwork for every loop, a valve for every gradient. And it meets a lab that writes its doubts beside its certainties, and breaks them on a schedule.

tagLine.canonical: TAG-LINE MAP (canonical): the copper line is a set, not a void: the tag-keeper's workshop, established in ch01-s05. L2 a tall paned window wall (its sky carries the mood); L3 the workbench with the HandwiredOS desk's silhouette and the parchment plates pinned along its back edge; L4 the copper line between two posts at 58% frame height; L5 the narrator's hands, always from lower left; L6 the near post at frame right, where the red pencil rests. The Lifespan Rule lies front-on along the bench edge under the line: log-scale ticks, labelled an hour · a day · a year · a lifetime (week, month and decade unlabelled). Tags hang left to right in the order they are tied (tag 1 at the far left, the blank why tag at the far right since ch01-s05) and never change places except in the ch12 re-hang. LIFESPAN ENCODING (one rule, film-wide; every tag's thread obeys it): a struck or ended thread drops to the rule at its measured lifespan and ends there in a cut, dull tip. A still-held thread drops to its age as of 27 October 2026 and ends in a glowing open tip with a short copper arrow pointing right. Nothing runs off the rule's end except a thread that really is older than a lifetime. Tip positions: tag 1 biology strand ended at about seventy-seven years (1943 to 2020), just short of 'a lifetime'; tag 1 engineering strand still held at about eighty-three years, the ONLY thread past 'a lifetime'; tag 2 still held at about seven and a half years (March 2019), between 'a year' and 'a lifetime', short of the decade tick; tag 6 still held at thirteen days (the README's small print, 14 October 2026), between a week and a month; tag 7 ended at about three months; tag 8 ended at about eight weeks; tag 9 ended within hours, between 'an hour' and 'a day'; tag 10 still held at thirteen days (14 October 2026), between a week and a month; tag 11 JSON strand still held at about twelve days (15 October), TOML strand ended at one to two days. Question cards (qK, why?, the nanoGPT question) never drop to the rule. Suspects 3, 4 and 5 hang slack with no drop (a suspect has no date to measure).

hands.canonical: HAND SIGNATURES (canonical, cast.json signatureLock): the narrator's hands enter from the lower LEFT and alone tie, flip, rivet, lift, place, bend and hold up; the red-pencil hand enters from frame RIGHT and only writes, strikes or rests; the author's hands appear only at a laptop or desk under a lamp; the agent's hand is a paper sheet paler, sits beside the author's, and never acts first; the viewer's hand is bare and rises from below, once (ch12-s06). No tag is tied, flipped, written, struck or riveted without a hand. chapters.title: Four and a Half
chapters.blurb: A copper thread becomes the wire under a paper desk. The desk is one neural network, and its Monitor window shows that network to itself: 234 state cells, 4,646 operations, 493 outputs, and a wallpaper with one arc for each of its 9,909 weights. The narrator ties the viewer's three likely guesses onto a copper line as suspect tags. Then the README's (a > 4) ? 10 : 12 is built from two ramps and a lever: five gives ten, three gives twelve, and four and a half gives eleven. The tag inks the README's own small print, "For an integer a". First full refrain, then the title.

shots.setting: Black void with low haze; a copper thread draws itself across the dark and becomes the copper wire under a paper dock (HandwiredOS, October 2026, no time of day: a stage before the lamps come up)
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: one copper thread draws itself across black and turns out to be the wire under a paper dock. Total black for a breath, then the haze lifts a little in the L1 backlight (parchment mood held very low, intensity 0.25, so the frame reads almost black with a warm floor). From frame left at 58% of frame height, a single copper thread (the film's copper line: 1.5 px core, a warm rim on its top edge, a soft halo) draws itself left to right like a slow fuse, with a tiny bright bead at its tip and the haze glowing faintly where it has passed. The camera holds still with the faintest drift (lens 1.00 to 1.02). At the 'dock' beat the line stops just past frame centre and three paper tiles fold up out of the dark above its right half (white rounded squares cut from card, rim-lit, each carrying a small cut-out glyph: a pulse line, a page, a picture), so we understand the copper thread is the wire running under the HandwiredOS dock. On the 'clack' beat, a single relay clack, and the wire's halo steps up once and settles. No narration, no type. This is the film's first image and, at the very end (ch12-s07), its last light.

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the desk is revealed as a toy theatre, and a dragged window glides and settles. The camera pulls back and up from the dock of the previous shot (lens 1.10 to 1.00 over the lead-in) to a wide on the HandwiredOS desk built as a paper toy theatre: a warm paper-beige desktop flat at L3 with a faint dot grid printed in ink at 8% (the real site's look: paper, ink and one copper accent), the copper wire running under the three-tile dock along the bottom. Three paper windows hang on fine threads from the top of the proscenium, each a sheet of card with a serif title strip: Monitor (left, its sidebar and a list of rows), Notes (centre right, a short to-do list in a pen-like hand, its LAST line deliberately soft and out of focus: the plant for ch12-s05; nothing in it is legible yet), Photos (right, a 4 x 3 grid of twelve tiny landscape cut-outs: hills, a lake, a tree line). On 'windows' each window gets a brief rim kick in turn; on 'dock' the three tiles lift a hair; on 'photographs' the twelve cells of the Photos grid catch light in reading order (twelve quick ticks). On 'Drag' a small paper cursor arrow (no hand: the narrator's hands first appear in ch01-s05) presses Photos' title bar and drags it left and down; the window follows; on release ('glides') it carries on alone along the same path, slowing; on 'settles' it eases to rest and its hanging threads swing once and still. The focused window carries a faint copper wash. No logos, no browser chrome. Small fog sheet B across the desk floor.

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: we push into Monitor and read the program's own numbers in its sidebar. The lamp warms from parchment to candleAmber as the camera pushes in (continuous dolly z 0 to +260 over the shot; the window grows to fill two thirds of the frame). Monitor is a paper sheet with a serif title strip; its sidebar heading, set in the window's own small type, reads THIS PROGRAM, with three figures under it: State 234, Operations 4,646, Outputs 493. On the right, Monitor's list of rows (the program's own cells and operations), each row a strip of card with a name stub and a live number; as the Photos window (still easing at frame edge) settles, a handful of the row values tick to new numbers on twos, so we see the list is the network's live state, not a picture of it. On 'network' the three sidebar figures get a brief warm kick; on 'live' the ticking numbers pulse once together. The footer strip along the bottom of the window reads 130 layers · 9,909 weights (show only these two figures: no byte count). Depth: the window at L4, the dimmed desk at L3, haze between. Ends still pushing, carrying straight into the next shot.

lines.text: Even the wallpaper maps it: one arc for each weight, each number it multiplies by. Nine thousand, nine hundred and nine.
lines.direction: wonder held in check; say the number slowly and evenly, each part its own step

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the camera passes through Monitor into a cathedral of arcs, one per weight. The push from the previous shot continues straight through the paper of the Monitor window (it parts like a stage gauze) into the desktop's wallpaper, staged as depth: all 9,909 thin semicircular arcs, cut from foil-thin card, hung on L1 to L4, most copper, some grey-blue indigo, each a hairline with a rim on its upper edge. The arcs are the real wallpaper's rule: each one runs from a value to the operation that reads it. A multiplane dolly drifts forward (z +260 to +700) and the near arcs part to either side like threads on a loom, the far ones haze toward the backlight. On 'arc' one copper arc and one indigo arc nearest the lens brighten for a beat each (the label lands with them). On 'thousand' the whole field brightens once, layer by layer from far to near, then settles. DATA BINDING (style bible §6): the arcs are generated, not hand-placed, from research/exports/handwiredos-circuit.json, the compiled HandwiredOS circuit exported from the pinned clone at 257856e (command: bun films/handwired-explained/tools/export-handwiredos-circuit.ts .orly-work/repos/handwired; run 2026-10-28, its totals match the bible: 234 source cells, 130 layers, 4,646 live operations, 9,909 stored weights, 2,776 ReGLU, 59 boolean, longest gate chain 71). One arc per entry of its arcs array, 9,909 in all, each drawn as src/handwiredos/wiring.ts draws it: from the value it reads to the operation that reads it, copper where the sign is +1 (adding) and indigo where it is -1 (subtracting). The far layers may thin to hairlines in the haze, but every arc is drawn and none is invented, so the label 9,909 arcs · one per weight is literally true. The same export drives the ch05 loom; the shots stage records the command and totals in sources.json. Nothing in the arcs moves except by camera and haze: they are a picture of the program, drawn from its wiring, not part of its computing. Fog sheet A drifts slowly left.

chapters.title: The Oldest Tags
chapters.blurb: Framing only, said once in narration: the repo never cites the 1943 work. In 1943 McCulloch and Pitts tie on the oldest tag, the neuron as logic; their units fire against fixed thresholds and learn nothing. In 1951 Kleene shows such a net is a finite machine whose patterns are regular events; the film's own reading: a finite net can only remember so much, so anything unbounded has to come from outside. In 2020, branches of a single human neuron are caught answering either input but not both (XOR), which no lone threshold gate can, and the tag's thread splits: as biology it frays, as engineering it never came down. A younger tag, 2019: learn the weights, don't write them, with Sutton for and Brooks against. Some kept writing weights anyway (Siegelmann and Sontag, Tracr, Giannou et al., Percepta). Then the echo, not lineage: eighty-three years on, someone has written a network's weights by hand to run a desktop.

chapters.blurb: June to September 2026. One lit window on a June night becomes a project with three names (two renames) in four months, and a second hand rests at the keyboard, unexplained. What a Handwired program really is: a fixed list of thirty-two-bit operations, appended by builder code that runs once; a table of numbered cells; four instructions and nothing else. Two of our own suspects fall: no tool converted ordinary code, and nobody trained it. A silent odd number is left on the instruction plate, and the Notes window is planted: the program holds no text.

chapters.title: Deep Dive I: Two Ramps and a Lever
chapters.blurb: The README's (a > 4) ? 10 : 12, worked by hand on one growing machine at a backlit workbench. A bend of copper becomes a ReLU ramp; two ramps and a lever make a bit; both belts always run and each shutter scales the tile it passes; infinity on the closed belt still poisons the tray. Four and a half gives five and six, fused into eleven; past two to the twenty-fourth a whole number gives twenty minus twelve, eight. Just below that edge, the odd number on the plate snaps a score to a bit in one instruction. What exact means, and why doubles broke things. Then the real library demands a promise about its input, shrinks the comparison to two operations, and gives eleven again when the promise is false: declarations are promises, not proofs. Promise only a range and a lens train magnifies by two to the hundred and forty-ninth. Sixteen against two, and a silent plant for later.

chapters.title: One Big Matmul
chapters.blurb: September to October 2026. The builder ribbon feeds the matmul loom: 130 thin frames, one per layer, copper threads adding and indigo subtracting, mostly empty air, every thread one real stored weight. A matmul is many weighted sums at once; some sums fold together, but nothing merges across a gate, and the longest chain of gates runs 71 deep. The third suspect is struck: it is a network in the plain sense. The loom's threads turn out to be the desk's wallpaper; when Notes hands its text back to the browser, the loom sheds most of them. And a furnace that should have been faster runs cold: everything here is JavaScript on the processor, and on a graphics card an older build ran fifteen to twenty-seven times slower. So what is a GPU for?

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the giant matmul revealed as a loom. CAMERA: starts tight on the BUILDER RIBBON from ch03-s02 (operation tags on a paper ribbon, each pinned one column right of its deepest input), which runs out of frame left; a slow lateral dolly follows the ribbon right until it feeds, like warp thread, into the MATMUL LOOM. The loom is a long run of 130 THIN UPRIGHT FRAMES receding in multiplane depth (L2 to L4), each frame a backlit paper lattice, one per layer. As the ribbon reaches the loom (on 'loom'), its tags drop off the ribbon into the frames by depth: every tag whose inputs are equally deep falls into the SAME frame, so frames fill side by side, not one after another (on 'layer', one tag drops into the first frame after the frames of the tags it reads, and two tags in one frame glow together with no thread between them: neither waits on the other). Between frames run fine THREADS OF LIGHT, one per stored weight: copper threads for adding weights, indigo (grey-blue) for subtracting, exactly the wallpaper's two colours (on 'Copper', the copper threads catch the rim; on 'Indigo', the indigo ones). Behind the frames, half in haze: small hinged ReLU ramps and a few toothed detent wheels, the gates that sit after the sums. On 'empty': the camera racks focus through one frame; it is a sparse lattice, a handful of threads crossing a big field of dark air, because each layer's matrix is mostly zeros. DATA BINDING (style bible §6): every thread, frame and gate fixture is drawn from the real compiled program, not illustrative density. Export it headlessly from a checkout of chenglou/handwired at 257856e: `createWindowManagerMachine()` from src/handwiredos/window-manager.ts, then its `tensorProgram`; per frame (layer) draw one thread per stored weight in `layer.weights` (indigo where the weight is negative, copper otherwise), each thread running from the value it reads (`layer.inputIndices[layer.columns[k]]`) to the operation that reads it, exactly as src/handwiredos/wiring.ts draws the wallpaper; mount a ReLU ramp for each row in `layer.gateRows` and a detent wheel for each row in `layer.booleanRows`. A summary export reportedly matched the bible's figures on 2026-10-28 (130 layers, 4,646 live operations, 9,909 weights, longest ReGLU/boolean chain 71 [OS02, CM07]); the shots stage runs the full export, films/handwired-explained/tools/export-handwiredos-circuit.ts, and checks those totals before drawing (meta staging.buildList.matmulLoom). The shots stage commits the export (JSON) beside the shot and records the command in sources.json; the ch01-s04 and ch05-s04 wallpaper arcs are generated from the same export. Haze drifts through the lattices; the loom never moves except for a faint shimmer along the threads, as if under tension.

chapters.title: Deep Dive II: The Clockwork That Cannot Stop
chapters.blurb: The host loop, springs and patterns. A program cannot stop early, so every loop must become a count, a tree, a table, or the same work on every item, and the four nouns become the four arms of a clockwork. One turn of the clock; springs squared into four numbers and fourteen operations; a ratchet that snaps at three hundred steps; two desks at ten and a hundred and twenty frames a second that match in every bit, in the repo's tests, because the frame you see is a rehearsal thrown away; tag 7 struck. Then the four shapes of a loop, each with its own machine, and two old names signed into the runtime, on screen. A finite machine paid off, an echo of Kleene and not a citation: the network is one fixed, exact step, and the host turns the crank.

On 'program', under the title a STRAIGHT, ONE-WAY STRIP OF PAPER TRACK draws itself left to right across the plate, with a row of small stations along it; a small paper bead sets off at the left and crosses at an even pace, passing EVERY station, never skipping one. Along the track sit three tiny empty sockets, where a jump, a break and a repeat would sit, visibly vacant (no exit ramp, no points, no way back); one small label under them reads no jump · no break · no repeat. As the voice names the four nouns, four brass ARMS swing out from the hub of a HOST CLOCKWORK silhouetted behind the plate (escapement, ratchet wheel, a crank), each arm's tip a different small machine-shape (a peg rail for the count, a forked thread for the tree, a drawer for the table, a row of identical tiles for the same work on every item): shapes, not words. chapters.title: Deep Dive III: Unfreezing
chapters.blurb: Gradients through a handwritten program. The README asks what happens if its frozen weights are let go. One ReGLU valve worked by hand, forward and backward: open at 0.15, out comes 0.225, slopes 0.45 and 1.5; lower one bias and the valve shuts, and every slope behind it goes dark. Almost every operation in the program runs backwards by a rule, on the real arithmetic, not the rounding. Tag 10, fully differentiable, is doubted from inside the repo: the decisions are flat. Then the one demo that really learns, the learned gallery: you sketch rectangles and 244 weights, from a seeded random start, learn to place the photos on them; a plain-JavaScript clerk deciding who goes where, every pull capped so that far-off photos vote rather than shout, 600 steps a second. A shortcut that snapped the sketch to a grid in ordinary code is refused. Honest scope: a small generic network, not a hand-written program unfrozen; the lab did unfreeze five design numbers (one gradient step solved nearly two moving drag frames in three; about one in four started with every slope at zero); the nanoGPT dream hangs as a question. And the desk's X-ray shows a single valve, dark.

chapters.title: The Summer's Certainties
chapters.blurb: July to mid-September 2026. The Window Calendar dims: six panes in July, and an August with no commits at all, which the record does not explain. The July briefs list established conclusions to be taken as given, tied on by a design conversation the repo never names. On 3 September a review run by an AI agent retires ten of them, and the dead end's narrower replacement is named (a defined numeric subset can be compiled), and three of its findings go on plates: a nought-out-of-twenty result that becomes twenty out of twenty when the error is multiplied by a million, because the optimiser's tiny safety constant was swamping the slopes; a checker that reported zero mismatches because it skipped the same early return as the compiled code; and, as a silent plate, a gradient that came out nought or three depending on operand order, fixed that morning with 274 tests passing. The film's one plain sentence about tooling: every commit authored by Cheng Lou, most also crediting a coding agent, and this film written with Claude; one process, under his direction. By mid-September three runtime questions are settled, September's panes relight, and the tag hangs struck after about eight weeks.

chapters.title: Four Days in October
chapters.blurb: 13 to 14 October 2026. The Window Calendar blazes: 689 commits in October, 683 of them in four days. A question from Cheng, and, weighing a million documents, a sentence that could be this film's motto: check before you build. JSON search gets its machine time: 100,000 documents, one GPU thread each, all running the same small step. Tag 9, the GPU is the faster one, is tied on at 09:01, already hedged. Then the test: a pattern written as cells, two forward passes because a program can't go back, and the browser's RegExp on one thread in its booth with a ten-second hourglass. A same-day review finds one of eighteen cores; given eight workers, RegExp keeps up back to back and wins after a pause, and the tag is struck: the shortest thread in the film. Then the go-ahead, and the repository goes public.

chapters.title: Strangers with Pencils
chapters.blurb: 20 to 27 October 2026. The world reads the tags. On Hacker News a commenter calls it a little language for building circuits, and another sees a compiler, and the docs side with the first: tag 4 was struck in the first minutes. A stranger tries four and a half and gets eleven; tag 6 is turned over, and its back was never blank: the landing page's hidden comment had said so. A promise that states its limits is kept. Another asks why, and that question is hung on the line for the end. Of the lab itself, no public word: the strangers' pencils were gentler than the lab's own.

chapters.blurb: Dawn, 27 October 2026. Every belief in the film hangs on the copper line across misty hills, its thread dropping to the Lifespan Rule at the time it held. Re-hung by the compiler's own layering rule, applied to the film's teaching order, the line becomes a loom; one wave of light runs through it, and the struck tags run too, multiplied by zero, the wave coming to rest on an empty hook. Three beliefs are still argued over, the README offers its nearest answers to a stranger's 'why?', and the Notes window's last line becomes an invitation: the empty hook's profile bent into a copper hinge, a blank tag on it, placed in the viewer's hand, the refrain left for once as open questions.

shots.visual: Open on the Still open drawer from ch11-s05, still open in the window bay (it never closes). The camera rises past it and out through the bay window onto MISTY HILLS AT DAWN: four or five paper ridges receding in dawnGold haze, each paler than the last. Across the valley the copper line is strung from post to post like a washing line, and on it hang all eleven Promise Tags, each in the state the film left it, its thread dropping to the Lifespan Rule, a long paper ruler with copper log-scale ticks hung FRONT-ON below the line, parallel to the picture plane (no perspective) (an hour · a day · a year · a lifetime labelled; week, month and decade ticks unlabelled, as in ch01-s07). ONE ENCODING, the bound variable of the whole film (as staging.tagLine): a struck or ended thread drops to the rule at its MEASURED LIFESPAN and ends there, frayed or cut; a still-held thread drops to its AGE AS OF 27 OCTOBER 2026 and ends in a glowing open tip with a short copper arrow pointing right (still growing). Nothing runs off the rule's end except the one strand that is truly older than a lifetime. Left to right in film order, with each tip: tag 1 split at the knot, its biology strand frayed and ended at about seventy-seven years (1943 to 2020, between the decade tick and 'a lifetime'), its engineering strand the ONLY thread that runs past 'a lifetime' (1943 to now, about eighty-three years), open glowing tip and arrow just beyond the rule's end; tag 2, still held, open tip and arrow at about seven and a half years (March 2019), between 'a year' and 'a lifetime', just short of the unlabelled decade tick, the red pencil resting on its post (contested); tags 3, 4 and 5, the three suspects, struck through once on slack threads; tag 6 riveted, still held, open tip and arrow at thirteen days (the README's small print, 14 October), between the week and month ticks; tag 7 struck, ended at about three months, frayed start; tag 8 struck with ten short red strokes on its back, ended at about eight weeks; tag 9 struck, its thread barely a millimetre long (hours); tag 10, still held, open tip and arrow at thirteen days (14 October), between the week and month ticks, beside tag 6's, with the small nanoGPT question tag hanging slack beneath it; tag 11, the border tag (JSON half riveted, TOML half struck, the bison thread ending in its open loop), split as ch11-s04 left it: its JSON strand still held, open tip and arrow at about twelve days (15 October), between the week and month ticks; its TOML strand ended at one to two days (15 to 16 October), between 'a day' and the week tick; and the small 'why?' question tag on its slack thread (a question, not a belief: no tip on the rule). In the far distance, on a ridge, the Window Calendar stands as a tall paper building, its panes dark after 16 October: no new panes light. Staging for 1280x720: the line and the Rule both run front-on, parallel to the picture plane. Slow lateral drift along them, left to right, so every tag passes once, about four tags legible in frame at a time (each tag about 110 px wide), never all twelve at once. The drift ends on a WIDE in which the tags are too small to read as words and read instead as STATES: split, glowing, struck, riveted, frayed, slack, and the copper arrows of the four still-held tips (1's engineering strand, 2, 6, 10) clearly pointing right. No new text except the date stamp. The tag fronts are legible but not re-read. Its short to-do list, out of focus since ch01-s02, racks into focus line by line from the top; on 'line' the rack reaches the bottom and the last line sharpens, in the window's own type (Q088), as part of the window itself; no caption repeats it, only a small attribution 'HandwiredOS · Notes'. Nothing else moves; Photos' twelve landscapes sit still.

lines.text: Who ties the next one on? Who doubts it? How long will it hold?
lines.direction: the refrain turned, the film's last thought, and the only time it is left unanswered: three open questions, soft, warm, unhurried, a real breath after each; no answer follows

lines.text: It's waiting for the next pair of hands.
lines.direction: the invitation, almost a smile; let 'hands' rest; nothing after it

shots.visual: Close on the copper wire under the dock. The narrator's hands enter lower left and BEND a short length of it into a hinge ('bend' action): flat, then up, a ReLU, the same emblem as the copper hinge in Deep Dive I and EXACTLY the profile of column 5's empty hook in ch12-s02 to s04, the frame the wave came to rest on; the bend is cut so the hinge's silhouette matches that glowing bare hook, and its bare end catches the same faint copper glow, so the waiting hook is paid. In the lead-in the hands tie the BLANK tag to the hinge (detent: tie), and flip it once (detent: flip) to show its back is blank too: no belief on the front, no name in the knot, no red pencil on the back. Each of the three questions is timed to the open hand: on 'ties' a plain, open hand (the viewer's: no sleeve, no ring, no age or gender signal) begins to rise into the lower third from below frame; on 'doubts' it is halfway up; on 'hold' it settles, palm up, still. On 'waiting' the narrator's hands place the hinge with its blank tag into that open palm ('place' action) and withdraw lower left. The open hand holds it, still. The red-pencil hand never appears. The third stroke of the detent never comes. Camera: locked off, then the slightest drift toward the palm as the last word lands.

music.note: the detent figure for the last time: tie (soft detent click), flip (paper snap), and the third stroke never comes; the bar hangs on one warm low line, intensity 0.2, decaying into room tone under the held palm. No cadence.

shots.visual: The frame darkens to black around the copper wire under the dock until it is the last light in frame, a thin warm line; a single relay clack, and it goes out. Fade up on a parchment end card: the as-of line, set plain, with the commit hash in monospace. Crossfade to a credits card in the house serif, then to one static sources card (the commit hash is on the end card; the sources card carries the address of the full list). No logos; no publisher's name; only the parody imprint 'O'RLY?' if any imprint appears at all. Fade to black.
